In the Book of Revelation, this is associated with the “number of the beast,” leading some community members to view the milestone as noteworthy and somewhat amusing in the project’s history. However, in reality, this was just a standard procedure from a technical standpoint. Cardano organizes its operations into so-called epochs, which are five-day periods consisting of 432,000 one-second slots. They help structure the overall activity, including transaction processing, rewarding, and staking. Once an epoch ends, the blockchain seamlessly moves on to the next one. Latest data shows that epoch 666 was successfully completed on November 10, and the network is currently progressing through epoch 667, which is expected to conclude on November 15. At balances and rates as of 9 November 2026, the changes add about $3.5M of annualised revenue to the DAO and raise the blended RF from 12.0% to 12.7%. The proposal is part of the ongoing effort to streamline Aave V3. Motivation Overview Over the past months, the DAO has been streamlining Aave V3. Low-adoption reserves and instances have been wound down, Aave V2 has been frozen, and ongoing work aims to focus Ethereum Core on liquid, bluechip collateral, with assets that carry additional risk moving to Aave V4, where that risk can be priced. This proposal applies the same direction to the protocol’s revenue side. Every borrowable reserve exposes the DAO to collateral, oracle and liquidation risk. The RF compensates the DAO for carrying that risk. On many reserves today, the DAO keeps a small share of the interest on positions whose tail risk it fully underwrites. events.excerpt: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.”
events.headline: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC

events.excerpt: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. events.excerpt: The Statistical Reality of Coding Agents For technical decision-makers, leaderboard order can look more conclusive than the underlying comparisons allow. The ExpertCrowd-SWE study , an author-reported coding-agent benchmark submitted on November 9, 2026, provides a nuanced look at seven frontier coding agents. Rather than a simple ranking, the study identifies four statistical tiers, highlighting where evidence separates models and where it remains inconclusive. Four tiers, not seven distinct places The paper evaluated seven models on 100 expert-authored software-engineering tasks drawn from 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. Each model attempted each task five times. The paper reports 3,495 scored runs. Gemini 3.8 Flash had no valid run on one assigned task, so its score covers 99 tasks. The reported averages are: Opus 5.5 (67.3%), GPT-6 Astra (63.7%), Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0% across 99 tasks), Qwen 3.8 Max (33.5%), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (32.5%), and Grok 4.6 (32.2%). These averages form a four-tier pattern. The bottom three models—Qwen, DeepSeek, and Grok—are not statistically separated from one another in pairwise comparisons. Similarly, the top two models, Opus and Astra, are not statistically separated. While Opus leads Astra by 3.6 percentage points,
events.headline: ExpertCrowd-SWE finds four coding-agent tiers, but top pair remains unresolved

events.excerpt: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. The Moscow Exchange is preparing a gradual pilot that starts in December. Crypto stays banned as a means of payment inside Russia, even as trading opens up. Russia’s stock exchanges will be legally allowed to run organized cryptocurrency trading from November 22 , 2026, after the Ministry of Justice registered a Bank of Russia ordinance setting out how trading in digital currencies and digital rights must work. The central bank confirmed the registration on November 11. November 22 is only the earliest legal opening date, since each exchange first needs the regulator to approve its trading rules, and the Moscow Exchange is aiming for December 1. For a central bank that wanted sweeping crypto restrictions less than five years ago, this puts Bitcoin on the same supervised venues where Russians already trade stocks and the ruble. Exchanges need their rulebooks approved first The ordinance builds on the conditions for organised trading in digital currencies that the Bank of Russia first drafted in July.
